why.correct: The efferent lymphatic vessel leaves the node at the hilum, the indented side, carrying lymph out. There are only one or two, compared with several afferent vessels.
options: Afferent lymphatic vessels enter all over the curved outer surface, not at the hilum.
Correct. A single vessel leaving at the hilum is the efferent lymphatic vessel.
High endothelial venules are small blood vessels in the paracortex, inside the node, where lymphocytes leave the blood.
A trabecula is a partition of connective tissue running inward from the capsule. It does not leave the node.

why.correct: The pale middle of a lymphoid nodule in the cortex is a germinal center, where lymphocytes that have met their antigen multiply rapidly.
options: Correct. A pale center inside a lymphoid nodule is a germinal center.
Medullary sinuses are channels between the medullary cords, deep in the node near the hilum, not the center of a round nodule in the cortex.
The subcapsular sinus is the narrow space just under the capsule, a thin rim around the whole node.
The paracortex is the deep cortex, a band beneath the nodules, not the center of a nodule.

why.correct: White pulp forms pale islands of lymphocytes around the central arteries of the spleen.
options: Red pulp is the dark tissue that fills the rest of the spleen, around the islands, with its venous sinuses.
A germinal center forms inside a lymphoid nodule when its lymphocytes multiply. The pinned island is the whole region of lymphocytes around a central artery.
Venous sinuses are the oval, leaky blood channels scattered through the red pulp.
Correct. A pale island around a central artery is white pulp.

why.correct: The thoracic duct runs up in front of the spine from the cisterna chyli to the left side of the neck. It is the largest lymphatic vessel.
options: The right lymphatic duct is a short vessel on the right side of the neck, not a long vessel running up the trunk.
Correct. The long duct in front of the spine is the thoracic duct.
The intestinal trunk is a short vessel in the abdomen that empties into the cisterna chyli. It does not run up through the chest.
The left subclavian vein is the blood vessel the thoracic duct empties into, running sideways under the collarbone.

why.correct: The right lymphatic duct drains only the right arm, the right side of the chest and the right side of the head and neck. It empties where the right internal jugular vein meets the right subclavian vein.
options: The thoracic duct drains the rest of the body, including the left arm and both legs, but not the right arm.
The cisterna chyli is a sac in the upper abdomen that collects lymph from the legs, pelvis and gut. It empties into the thoracic duct, not directly into a vein.
The thoracic duct empties on the left side, and it does not drain the right arm.
Correct. Lymph from the right arm travels through nodes in the right armpit, the right subclavian trunk and the right lymphatic duct.

why.correct: Filtered fluid enters a blind-ended lymphatic capillary, travels in valved collecting vessels through the groin nodes, joins a lumbar trunk and the cisterna chyli, and rises in the thoracic duct to the left venous junction.
Efferent lymphatic vessels leave at the hilum, the indented side of the node, not the curved surface. Only the afferent vessels enter on the curved surface.
options: This step is right. Several afferent vessels enter all over the curved surface.
This step is right. The subcapsular sinus is the first space lymph enters.
This step is right. The sinuses are lined with macrophages that engulf what the lymph carries.
This is the error. Efferent vessels leave at the hilum.
This step is right. Lymph often passes through several nodes in a chain before reaching a trunk.

why.correct: Collecting vessels pass through lymph nodes, which filter the lymph, before merging into lymphatic trunks.
options: Blood capillaries are where fluid first leaves the blood. Lymph does not re-enter blood vessels until the ducts empty into the veins at the base of the neck.
Correct. Lymph is filtered by nodes along the collecting vessels.
The spleen has no afferent lymphatic vessels. It filters blood, not lymph.
The thymus is where one line of lymphocytes matures. Lymph does not flow through it on its way to the ducts.

why.correct: Losing the spleen removes a blood filter and a platelet reserve. Platelets and aging red cells rise in the blood, and defense against bacteria in the blood weakens for life, while the lymph nodes, which filter lymph, are unaffected.

variables.name: Platelet count in the blood
variables.why: The spleen normally holds about a third of the platelets in reserve. Without it, those platelets stay in the circulating blood, and fewer are removed.

variables.name: Number of old or misshapen red blood cells circulating
variables.why: Red pulp macrophages normally catch stiff, aging red cells that cannot squeeze through the slits into the venous sinuses. Without that squeeze test, more of them stay in circulation.

variables.name: Risk of an overwhelming bloodstream infection with sugar-coated bacteria
variables.why: Red pulp macrophages and white pulp lymphocytes are the main defense against bacteria in the blood, especially sugar-coated ones that are hard to engulf elsewhere. The liver takes over only part of the job.

variables.name: Filtering of lymph by lymph nodes
variables.why: The spleen filters blood, not lymph: it has no afferent lymphatic vessels. The lymph nodes keep filtering lymph as before.

why.correct: The endothelial cells of lymphatic capillaries overlap loosely. Fluid pushing in opens gaps large enough for proteins, and the flaps close behind them. Lymph then carries the protein back to the blood.
options: Correct. Loose, overlapping endothelial flaps let protein into lymphatic capillaries, where blood capillaries would hold it out.
Tissue cells do not pump albumin into capillaries. Proteins return to the blood through the lymphatic route.
Macrophages do engulf debris, but they do not clear the steady stream of plasma protein. Protein that stays in tissue draws in fluid and causes swelling.
Fluid and protein enter the lymphatic system at the capillaries. Collecting vessels carry lymph onward; their valves stop backflow rather than taking up protein.

why.correct: Primary lymphoid organs are where lymphocytes are made and mature: the red bone marrow and the thymus. The others are secondary lymphoid organs, where mature lymphocytes meet antigens.
options: Correct. One main line of lymphocytes matures in the thymus.
The spleen is a secondary lymphoid organ: its white pulp is where lymphocytes meet antigens in the blood.
Correct. Every lymphocyte is made in the red marrow, and one main line matures there.
The palatine tonsils are MALT, a secondary lymphoid tissue where lymphocytes meet antigens entering through the mouth.
Lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs, where lymphocytes meet antigens carried in lymph.

why.correct: Her capillaries filter at a normal rate, but the lymphatic route out of the arm was removed. Fluid and protein stay in the tissue, and white blood cells drawn into the stagnant fluid release signals that drive fibrosis and fat buildup, which is why the swelling has become firm and barely pits. This is secondary lymphedema.
options: Nothing in her story raises capillary pressure or makes the capillaries leakier. Her filtration is normal; drainage has failed.
Correct. With the armpit nodes and their vessels gone, the arm cannot return what it filters.
Her albumin is normal, and a low plasma protein would cause swelling in both legs and elsewhere, not in one arm.
A blocked vein raises capillary pressure and causes low-protein, pitting edema. Her surgery removed lymphatic drainage, and the firm, protein-rich swelling fits that.

why.correct: The spleen filters blood: its red pulp macrophages remove bacteria as blood squeezes from the cords into the venous sinuses, and its white pulp lymphocytes meet antigens in the blood.
options: Lymph nodes filter lymph, which carries what enters the tissues. Bacteria placed straight into the blood bypass them.
The thymus is where lymphocytes mature. It does not filter blood or lymph.
The palatine tonsils sample what enters through the mouth, not the blood.
Correct. The spleen is the lymphoid organ that filters blood.

why.correct: The paired palatine tonsils sit on each side at the back of the mouth.
options: The pharyngeal tonsil is a single tonsil high on the back wall of the throat, behind the nose. When enlarged it is called the adenoids.
The lingual tonsil lies at the back of the tongue, not on the side walls of the mouth.
Correct. These are the palatine tonsils.
Peyer's patches are lymphoid nodules in the wall of the intestine, not in the mouth.

why.correct: High endothelial venules in the paracortex are where circulating lymphocytes leave the blood and enter a node. If lymphocytes cannot stick to them, fewer lymphocytes enter the nodes, although lymph keeps flowing through.
options: Correct. Lymphocytes enter nodes from the blood by sticking to and squeezing between the tall endothelial cells of these venules.
Lymph enters through the afferent lymphatic vessels, which are unaffected. The venules are blood vessels.
The macrophages lining the sinuses engulf by phagocytosis. Blocking lymphocyte entry from the blood does not stop them.
Lymph leaves through the efferent vessels at the hilum. The venules do not control where lymph exits.

why.correct: The nodes under the jaw drain the throat. Lymphocytes in them meet antigens from the infection, multiply in germinal centers, and are held in the node, so it swells within days and becomes tender.
options: Cancer in a node usually causes a hard, painless node that keeps growing. A tender node during a sore throat fits an infection.
Nothing suggests blocked vessels. Swelling during an infection comes from lymphocytes multiplying and being held in the node.
Old red blood cells are removed mainly in the red pulp of the spleen, not in lymph nodes, and that would not cause swelling during an infection.
Correct. Lymphocytes multiplying in the node make it swell.

why.correct: Lymph has no heart. Besides the contraction of their own valved segments, lymphatic vessels (and leg veins) rely on the skeletal muscle pump. A still leg moves less lymph and venous blood, so fluid collects in the tissue.
options: Correct. Contracting calf muscles squeeze lymphatic vessels and veins; a still leg drains poorly.
Less filtration would reduce swelling, not cause it.
A cast does not remove lymph nodes. The nodes are intact; the lymph is simply moving slowly.
The red pulp is in the spleen and filters blood cells. It has nothing to do with fluid drainage from the leg.

why.correct: MALT is lymphoid tissue lying under mucous membranes: the tonsils, Peyer's patches, the appendix and BALT in the airways. The spleen and thymus are separate, encapsulated organs.
options: Correct. Peyer's patches are lymphoid nodules under the lining of the intestine.
Correct. The wall of the appendix is thick with lymphoid nodules beneath its mucous membrane.
The spleen is a separate organ with a capsule that filters blood. It does not lie in a mucous membrane.
Correct. The lingual tonsil lies under the mucous membrane at the back of the tongue.
Correct. BALT lies in the walls of the airways.
The thymus is a primary lymphoid organ in the chest, with a capsule. It is not part of a mucous membrane.

why.correct: With more vessels coming in than going out and a wide network of sinuses between, lymph moves slowly through the node. The extra time lets macrophages lining the sinuses engulf bacteria, debris and cancer cells.
options: The layout slows lymph rather than speeding it. The node is a filter, and a filter works better when flow is slow.
Lymph nodes do not add red blood cells to lymph; red cells stay in the blood vessels of the node.
Correct. Slow flow gives the macrophages time to clear the lymph.
The reverse is closer to the truth: capillaries in the node take back water, and lymph leaves richer in lymphocytes, not poorer.

why.correct: A healthy red cell folds and slips through the slits. An aging or deformed red cell is stiff, gets stuck in the cords, and is engulfed by red pulp macrophages. Its iron is recycled.
options: Correct. Stiff cells get stuck and are removed.
Young red cells are flexible and pass through the slits easily.
Lymphocytes collect in the white pulp; the red pulp does not return them to lymph, since the spleen has no afferent lymphatic vessels.
Albumin is a dissolved protein, not a cell. It passes through with the plasma.

why.correct: Innate defenses, such as neutrophils, macrophages and complement, are ready before any exposure and recognize features shared by whole groups of microbes, so they act within minutes to hours of a first encounter.
options: Antibodies against a new antigen take about a week to appear on first exposure, because the lymphocytes that make them must first be selected and multiply.
Lymphocyte memory exists only after a previous exposure. This is the first time.
Correct. Innate defenses are ready at birth and do not need earlier exposure.
Only adaptive immunity takes days on first exposure. The innate layer acts in minutes to hours.

why.correct: Cytokines make the endothelium sticky; the neutrophil rolls, then sticks firmly, squeezes out between endothelial cells, follows the chemical gradient to the bacteria, and engulfs them.

At A the set point has jumped to 39 °C but body temperature is still lower. The hypothalamus treats that gap exactly like cold: sympathetic signals constrict skin vessels, so the skin is pale and cool, and skeletal muscles shiver. The patient feels chilled.
options: Correct. Body temperature is below the raised set point, so heat-gain responses run.
Sweating and flushing are heat-loss responses. They happen at C, when body temperature is above a set point that has dropped.
The two lines match at B, not at A. At A the solid line is still below the dashed one.
Panting is a heat-loss response, and at A the body is gaining heat, not losing it.

why.correct: Once pyrogens are cleared, prostaglandin E2 falls and the set point returns to about 36.6 °C. Body temperature is now above the set point, so the hypothalamus dilates skin vessels and triggers sweating, and temperature falls until the two match again.
options: Control is working normally throughout: body temperature follows the set point up and then down, as negative feedback should.
Correct. Temperature is above the new, lower set point, so the body actively loses heat.
The fall is not passive. The graph shows temperature above the set point, which triggers active heat loss by sweating and skin vasodilation.
The dashed line has stepped down at hour 10, not up.

why.correct: Ibuprofen blocks prostaglandin E2 in the hypothalamus, so the set point drops below body temperature. Skin vessels dilate and sweating starts, and temperature falls. The infection itself is unchanged.

variables.name: Hypothalamic set point
variables.why: Pyrogens raise the set point through prostaglandin E2 in the hypothalamus. Blocking its synthesis lets the set point fall back toward normal.

variables.name: Blood flow to the skin
variables.why: Body temperature is now above the lowered set point, so sympathetic constriction of skin vessels eases and they dilate.

variables.name: Sweating
variables.why: With body temperature above the set point, the hypothalamus triggers heat loss, including sweating.

variables.name: Core body temperature
variables.why: Heat loss now exceeds heat production, so temperature falls toward the new set point.

variables.name: Number of bacteria at the infection site
variables.why: The drug acts on the set point, not on the bacteria. Lowering a fever does not by itself kill them.

why.correct: C5b gathers C6, C7, C8 and C9 into the membrane attack complex. Without C7 the pore cannot form. Neisseria bacteria depend on it most, which is why people lacking C5 to C9 suffer repeated Neisseria infections while coping with most other bacteria.
options: C3b is made before C7 is needed, so opsonization still works. That is why she handles most bacteria normally.
C3a and C5a are split off earlier in the cascade, before C7 joins, so inflammation and neutrophil attraction still work.
Correct. C7 is part of the membrane attack complex, which Neisseria are especially vulnerable to.
The classical pathway starts with the first complement protein binding antibodies. C7 acts at the end of the cascade, not the start.

why.correct: All three pathways converge on splitting C3. Without it there is no C3b to opsonize bacteria, no C3a, and no way to go on to C5 and the attack complex. People who lack C3 have severe infections with many kinds of bacteria from early childhood.
options: Correct. C3 is where every pathway meets, and C3b coating is complement's most important job.
C9 is needed only for the attack complex. Opsonization and inflammation still work without it.
Losing the lectin pathway leaves the classical and alternative pathways, which can still split C3.
Without C5 there is no C5a and no attack complex, but C3b opsonization, the most important function, still works.

why.correct: Complement opsonizes microbes (C3b), promotes inflammation and attracts neutrophils (C3a and C5a), and bursts microbes with the membrane attack complex. Fever and antiviral protection come from cytokines and interferons.
options: Correct. This is opsonization by C3b.
Correct. C3a and C5a trigger mast cells to release histamine.
Correct. C5a is a strong attractant for neutrophils.
Correct. The membrane attack complex forms a pore and the cell bursts.
The set point is raised by pyrogens such as interleukin-1 acting through prostaglandin E2, not by complement.
That is the job of interferons, which make neighboring cells produce antiviral proteins.

why.correct: The self-identity protein is an NK cell's "leave me alone" signal. A cell that has lost it, especially one also showing stress proteins, tips the balance toward killing. The NK cell releases granules: one protein forms pores, and enzymes enter and trigger apoptosis.
options: NK cells work the other way round: they kill cells that lack the normal self signal. Losing it hides a cell from some lymphocytes, but exposes it to NK cells.
NK cells kill by releasing granules onto the target, not by engulfing it.
NK cells do not make antibodies. Antibodies come from cells descended from a different line of lymphocytes.
Correct. Missing the self signal makes the cell a target, and it dies by apoptosis.

why.correct: After engulfing, a phagocyte normally consumes a burst of oxygen to make superoxide and then hydrogen peroxide and bleach. No extra oxygen use and microbes that survive inside point to a failed oxidative burst. This is chronic granulomatous disease.
options: His neutrophils reach infections normally, so chemotaxis works.
The problem is killing inside the vesicle, not moving vesicles to the cell surface. Engulfing works.
Neutrophils arrive at his infections, so they must be leaving the blood by diapedesis.
Correct. The missing jump in oxygen use shows the oxidative burst has failed.

why.correct: Interleukin-1 is a pyrogen. At leaky spots in the blood–brain barrier, it makes cells in the hypothalamus produce prostaglandin E2, which raises the set point.
options: Histamine acts locally at the site of inflammation. It is not the step that raises the set point.
Complement pores are aimed at microbes; your own cells carry regulator proteins that block them. They play no part in fever.
Interferon makes cells resist viruses. It is not the link between pyrogens and the set point.
Correct. Prostaglandin E2 is the messenger that raises the set point, which is why drugs that block its synthesis lower a fever.

why.correct: When the set point rises, body temperature is below it, not above it. The hypothalamus responds as if you were cold: it constricts skin vessels and starts shivering. Skin vessels dilate only later, when the set point falls again.
options: This step is right. Pyrogens from macrophages start most fevers.
This step is right. Prostaglandin E2 is the messenger that resets the hypothalamus.
This step is right. The set point, not the control system, is what changes.
This is the error. Body temperature is below the raised set point, so skin vessels constrict.
This step is right. Heat-gain responses raise temperature until it matches the new set point.

why.correct: Type I interferons are paracrine signals. They bind receptor proteins on nearby cells and switch on genes for antiviral proteins, which block viral protein synthesis and break down viral RNA if a virus later gets in. The infected cell itself is usually lost; its neighbors are protected.
options: Correct. Interferon warns neighboring cells, which then resist the virus.
Interferon does not attack virus particles directly. It acts on cells.
Coating a microbe for phagocytes is opsonization, done by C3b, not by interferon.
Fever is raised by pyrogens acting through prostaglandin E2. Interferon's main job is making cells resist viruses.

why.correct: Lysozyme is an enzyme in tears, saliva, mucus and neutrophil granules that breaks bonds in the bacterial cell wall. Without the wall, water rushes in and the bacterium bursts.
options: Defensins punch holes in microbial membranes; they are not enzymes that digest the cell wall.
Interferons act on your own cells to protect them from viruses. They do not attack bacteria.
C9 is part of the membrane attack complex in plasma, not an enzyme in tears.
Correct. Lysozyme digests bacterial cell walls.

why.correct: Intact skin is a dry, acidic, constantly shed layer of keratin-filled cells that bacteria cannot cross. A deep burn destroys that surface barrier, so bacteria living on the skin reach the tissues and blood.
options: Correct. The burn destroyed the skin barrier, the first line of defense.
Tears protect the eyes. They play no part in keeping skin bacteria out of the blood.
The cilia protect the airways. The bacteria came from his skin, not his lungs.
The set point controls temperature. It does not keep bacteria out of the body.

why.correct: Histamine makes the endothelial cells of capillaries and venules pull apart. Plasma proteins leak out, the oncotic difference that holds fluid in the blood shrinks, and fluid filters out faster. Dilated arterioles raise capillary pressure too.
options: Neutrophils take hours to arrive, and the number of cells is small compared with the volume of leaked fluid.
Pus forms over a day or more, as neutrophils die. The swelling here appears within minutes.
Correct. Leaky vessel walls let protein and fluid pour into the tissue within minutes.
Your own cells carry regulator proteins that stop the attack complex forming on them.

why.correct: Neutrophils die at the site within a day or two. Their bodies, dead and living microbes, tissue debris and leaked plasma make the thick yellow-white fluid called pus.
options: A clot is fibrin with trapped blood cells, not the creamy fluid that collects in an infected wound.
Correct. Pus is mostly dead neutrophils with microbes, debris and fluid.
Mucus is made by mucous membranes and is not the fluid of an infected wound in skin or deeper tissue.
Fat is not the main component of pus.

why.correct: Cytokines from macrophages at the wound act locally on the vessels and travel in the blood to the bone marrow, the hypothalamus and the liver. The result is a leaky, swollen wound, more circulating neutrophils, a fever and a rise in liver-made inflammatory proteins.

variables.name: Permeability of venules at the wound
variables.why: Histamine, prostaglandins, complement fragments and cytokines make the endothelial cells pull apart, so plasma and protein leak into the tissue.

variables.name: Neutrophil count in the blood
variables.why: Cytokines reaching the bone marrow make it release stored neutrophils, including young band cells, so the count rises.

variables.name: Core body temperature
variables.why: Interleukin-1 and other pyrogens make the hypothalamus produce prostaglandin E2, raising the set point; heat-gain responses then raise body temperature.

variables.name: C-reactive protein in the blood
variables.why: Cytokines reaching the liver make it release C-reactive protein and other proteins of inflammation into the blood.

why.correct: Chronic inflammation lasts weeks to years because the trigger, here silica that macrophages cannot digest, keeps going. Macrophages and lymphocytes dominate, new vessels grow, and fibroblasts lay down collagen, scarring the tissue.
options: Acute inflammation is dominated by neutrophils and lasts hours to days. This tissue has few neutrophils and years of scarring.
Correct. Macrophages, lymphocytes and fibrosis after years of exposure mark chronic inflammation.
An abscess is a walled-off pocket of pus, mostly dead neutrophils. This biopsy has few neutrophils.
Normal lung has few inflammatory cells and little collagen between its air sacs.

why.correct: Double-stranded RNA inside a cell is a pattern made when many viruses copy themselves; your own cells do not normally make it in the cytosol. Detecting it switches on type I interferon release, which protects neighboring cells.
options: Correct. Viral RNA in the cytosol triggers interferon release.
A bacterium on the surface would be detected by surface pattern recognition receptors that bind bacterial wall or flagellum molecules, not by cytosolic sensors for double-stranded RNA.
Normal cell division does not put double-stranded RNA in the cytosol, which is why its presence is an alarm signal.
Worms are far too large to get inside a cell, and they are not detected by sensors for viral RNA.

why.correct: Fever-reducing drugs work by blocking prostaglandin synthesis, which lowers a set point raised by pyrogens. In overheating from exercise, the set point is already normal; the body is losing heat as hard as it can and still falling behind. He needs active cooling.
options: Correct. With a normal set point, there is nothing for the drug to lower.
He has no infection, so there are no pyrogens driving his temperature up.
The drug acts on the set point, not directly on shivering or sweating.
His set point has not been raised. His body temperature is above a normal set point, which is why he is sweating heavily.

why.correct: The small patch of the antigen that one receptor protein binds is an antigenic determinant, also called an epitope. The protein in the figure has several, each bound by a different lymphocyte's receptor.
options: Correct. The patch an antigen receptor binds is an epitope (antigenic determinant).
An MHC protein is a membrane glycoprotein on your own cells that holds a peptide. It is not part of the antigen.
The antigen receptor is on the lymphocyte, drawn as the paired arms. The pinned patch is on the antigen they bind.
A hapten is a small molecule that becomes antigenic only when attached to one of your proteins. The pinned patch is part of a large protein antigen.

why.correct: A large protein has many epitopes on its surface. Each is recognized by different lymphocytes, so the one protein selects many clones at once: a polyclonal response.
options: The antigen does not reshape itself or the antigen receptors. Receptors are made at random in advance, and the antigen selects those that already fit.
Each lymphocyte and its clone carry one receptor specificity. Many clones, not one changing clone, explain the variety.
Nothing suggests contamination. Even a pure protein carries many epitopes.
Correct. Many epitopes on one antigen select many clones.

why.correct: Proteins made inside a cell, including viral ones, are chopped into peptides in the cytosol, loaded onto MHC class I in the endoplasmic reticulum and shown on the surface. Nearly every nucleated cell, liver cells included, does this, so T cells of the killing kind can spot the infected cell.
options: T cell receptors do not bind free antigen. They bind only peptides held on MHC proteins.
MHC class II is found on antigen-presenting cells and displays material taken in from outside, not proteins made in an ordinary liver cell's cytosol.
Correct. Class I shows what a cell makes inside itself.
T cells do not recognize complement. Their antigen receptors bind peptide on MHC.

why.correct: Mature red blood cells have lost their nucleus and organelles, so they cannot make new MHC class I or load peptides onto it. A parasite inside them, such as the one that causes malaria, is hidden from T cells that read class I; other defenses, such as the spleen's red pulp, must catch the infected cells.
options: Correct. With no nucleus and no endoplasmic reticulum, a red cell cannot make or load class I, so infected red cells escape T cell detection.
Membrane thickness is not the reason, and complement does not replace T cell recognition of what is inside a cell.
Red blood cells are not antigen-presenting cells and do not carry MHC class II.
Red blood cells cannot make class I at all, infected or not.

why.correct: The antigen-presenting cells are dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells. They take in material from outside and display its peptides on MHC class II.
options: Correct. Dendritic cells are the most important antigen-presenting cells, and they start almost every naive T cell response.
Correct. Macrophages show what they have swallowed on class II.
Correct. B cells take in the antigen their antigen receptors bind and show its peptides on class II.
Red blood cells carry almost no class I and no class II.
Neutrophils engulf microbes but are not antigen-presenting cells; they do not normally carry class II.
Muscle fibers carry class I, like other nucleated cells, but not class II.

why.correct: The dendritic cell captures the bacteria, processes them into peptides in lysosome-fused vesicles, loads the peptides onto class II, and carries them through the lymph to the node's paracortex, where the rare naive T cell with a matching antigen receptor finds them.
T cells are made in the marrow, travel as thymocytes to the thymus cortex, pass positive selection there, pass negative selection mostly in the medulla, and leave as naive T cells.

The thymus is where T cells mature, so without it T cells and the paracortex they fill are depleted. B cells, made in the marrow, and innate cells such as neutrophils are produced normally, though B cells get less T cell help.

variables.name: Number of mature T cells in the blood
variables.why: T cells mature in the thymus. Without it, thymocytes from the marrow have nowhere to go through positive and negative selection, so few mature T cells appear.

variables.name: Lymphocytes in the paracortex of the lymph nodes
variables.why: The paracortex is where T cells gather. With few T cells, it is nearly empty.

variables.name: Production of B cells in the bone marrow
variables.why: B cells are made and mature in the red bone marrow, which is normal.

variables.name: Neutrophil killing of bacteria by phagocytosis
variables.why: Neutrophils are innate cells made in the marrow and do not depend on the thymus.

why.correct: T cells recognize peptides only when held on self MHC. An antigen receptor that cannot bind self MHC at all could never recognize anything, so the thymocyte gets no survival signal and dies of neglect. This is positive selection.
options: Being unable to attack self is not enough; the cell must also be able to use self MHC. Without that, it is useless and is not kept.
It never leaves. Only thymocytes that pass both positive and negative selection are released.
Memory cells form only after a mature lymphocyte meets its antigen and expands. A thymocyte has not.
Correct. Failing positive selection means death by apoptosis.

why.correct: Receptors are made at random before any antigen is met, and they do not change to fit a new antigen. The antigen selects the cells that already fit. That is the core idea of clonal selection.
options: This step is right. Random joining of gene pieces makes each lymphocyte's receptor unique.
This is the error. The antigen selects existing receptors; it does not reshape them.
This step is right. Dendritic cells present viral peptides in the lymph node paracortex.
This step is right. This is clonal selection.
This step is right. This is clonal expansion.

why.correct: After selection, the lymphocyte divides every 6 to 8 hours for several days, producing a clone of identical cells. That clone supplies both the fighting cells and the memory cells.
options: Correct. Clonal expansion follows selection.
Deletion happens to self-reactive thymocytes during maturation, not to mature lymphocytes that meet a foreign antigen.
Anergy follows binding without the second, confirming signal, as with self antigen on resting dendritic cells. It would stop the response, not continue it.
Each cell keeps its antigen receptor specificity; its clone carries the same antigen receptor.

why.correct: A naive T cell needs two signals: its antigen receptor binding peptide on MHC, and a confirming signal from a dendritic cell that has detected danger. Binding without the second signal makes it unresponsive for a long time. This clonal anergy is part of peripheral tolerance.
options: Switching on needs the second signal, which a resting dendritic cell does not give. Attack would require tolerance to fail.
The dendritic cell displays normal MHC class I and shows no stress proteins, so NK cells leave it alone.
Mature T cells do not return to the thymus to be retested. Tolerance out in the body is peripheral tolerance.
Correct. Binding without a confirming signal causes anergy.

why.correct: Her first infection left memory B and T cells: far more numerous than the original naive cells, long-lived, and quick to switch on. When the virus returned, they responded within a day or two and cleared it before she felt ill.
options: Innate immunity recognizes patterns shared by groups of microbes and does not become specific to one virus.

The antibody molecules made at age 5 were broken down within weeks. Any antibody in her blood now is newly made by cells left from that first response, and her memory cells add a fast, strong new response.
Her MHC proteins are inherited and do not change. Losing the ability to present the virus would make her more vulnerable, not less.
Correct. Immunological memory rests on memory cells.

why.correct: Each child inherits one of each parent's two sets of MHC genes. The chance that a brother inherited the same set from the mother (1 in 2) and the same set from the father (1 in 2) is 1 in 4. An unrelated donor, drawn from tens of thousands of MHC versions, is far less likely to match.
options: Correct. Two independent 1-in-2 chances give 1 in 4.
Only identical twins always match. Other siblings inherit sets independently.
MHC genes are not on the sex chromosomes, so sex does not decide a match.
Parents and children share only one set, so they are half matches, and MHC varies between family members.

why.correct: B cell receptors, membrane-bound antibodies, bind epitopes on intact antigens free in fluid. T cells can recognize the venom only after an antigen-presenting cell has processed it and displayed its peptides on MHC.
options: T cell receptors bind only peptides held on MHC proteins, not free proteins in plasma.
Thymocytes are immature T cells in the thymus; they do not respond to antigens in the plasma.
Correct. B cells bind intact, free antigen directly.
NK cells carry no antigen receptor. They check other cells for stress proteins and missing MHC class I.

why.correct: T cells recognize short, linear peptides cut from proteins and displayed on MHC. Processing breaks the protein apart, so a stretch buried inside the folded protein can end up in an MHC groove.
options: B cell receptors bind epitopes on the surface of intact antigens, so a buried stretch is out of reach.
Antibodies, like B cell receptors, bind the surface of intact antigens.
Correct. Processing exposes buried stretches as peptides on MHC.
Complement binds surfaces, antibodies or microbial sugars, not buried parts of a protein, and it recognizes no specific epitope.

why.correct: Dendritic cells arriving through afferent lymph settle in the paracortex, the T cell zone, and naive T cells enter the node there through high endothelial venules. The two meet in the paracortex.
options: Germinal centers form in the nodules of the cortex, where activated B cells multiply.
The subcapsular sinus is where lymph first enters; dendritic cells pass through it on their way to the paracortex.
The efferent vessel carries lymph out of the node, after it has passed the lymphocytes.
Correct. The paracortex is the T cell zone where dendritic cells present.

why.correct: Memory cells are a larger, longer-lived and quicker-to-respond version of the clone that met the antigen. They keep the same specificity.
options: Correct. Clonal expansion leaves 100 to 1,000 times more matching cells.
Correct. They respond within a day or two instead of about a week.
Correct. Some last for decades.
They belong to the same clone, so they carry the same antigen receptor and recognize the same epitope.
They carry the clone's antigen receptor; that is how they recognize the antigen again.

why.correct: Negative selection removes thymocytes that bind self peptides strongly, but only for self peptides the thymus displays. Without AIRE, organ-specific proteins are missing from the medulla, so T cells that react to them are never deleted and later attack those organs.
options: Positive selection checks only whether a thymocyte can bind self MHC. It does not remove self-reactive cells.
Correct. Central tolerance failed because the self proteins were never shown in the medulla.
Clonal expansion happens after a mature cell is selected by antigen. The problem is that the self-reactive cells survived maturation.
Processing in the skin concerns antigens met out in the body. The failure here is in the thymus, where tolerance to the parathyroid is normally built.

why.correct: B cells are made and finish maturing in the red bone marrow, where self-reactive ones are removed or change their antigen receptor.
options: The thymus is where T cells mature.
The spleen is a secondary lymphoid organ where mature B cells meet blood-borne antigens.
Correct. B cells mature in the red bone marrow.
Lymph nodes are secondary lymphoid organs where mature B cells gather in the nodules of the cortex.

why.correct: Peptides made inside a cell are displayed on MHC class I, which nearly every nucleated cell carries. CD8 binds MHC class I, so a CD8 cytotoxic T cell recognizes the infected cell and kills it.
options: A liver cell is not an antigen-presenting cell and carries little MHC class II. Class II shows engulfed material, not proteins the cell makes itself.
Correct. Internal (here viral) peptides go on MHC class I, and CD8 pairs with class I.
CD4 binds MHC class II, not class I, so a CD4 T cell cannot lock onto this complex.
The pairing is reversed. CD8 binds class I; MHC class II is recognized with CD4.

why.correct: CD4 is the coreceptor protein on helper T cells. It clamps onto the MHC class II protein beside the T cell receptor.
options: CD8 is on cytotoxic T cells and binds MHC class I. It is labeled in the lower panel, on the cytotoxic T cell, not on the helper T cell.
MHC II is on the dendritic cell, holding the antigen. The pinned protein is on the T cell.
Correct. CD4 on the helper T cell binds MHC class II.
The T cell receptor grips the antigen in the MHC groove. The pinned protein sits beside it and binds the MHC protein itself.

why.correct: Perforins are released from the cytotoxic T cell's granules. They insert into the target cell's membrane and form pores that let granzymes in.
options: Cytokines are the signals released by the helper T cell in the upper panel. They direct other cells; they do not kill.
Correct. Perforins make pores in the infected cell's membrane.
Antibodies are released by cells descended from B cells, not by cytotoxic T cells.
Antigens are pinned inside the infected cell. The pinned molecules are released by the T cell.

why.correct: Activated T cells make IL-2, which drives them to divide again and again. Without IL-2, T cells that recognize donor HLA cannot build the large clones of effector cells that destroy the graft. Off the drug, clonal expansion resumes and rejection follows.
options: Acute rejection is driven by T cells, and ABO antibodies cause hyperacute rejection within minutes. The drug acts on T cell IL-2.
Recognition (signal 1) still happens on the drug. What is blocked is the IL-2 that turns recognition into expansion.
Neutrophils are innate cells and do not use IL-2 to expand. The drug's target is T cell activation.
Correct. Blocking IL-2 blocks clonal expansion of the T cells that react to donor HLA.

why.correct: T cell activation needs recognition and costimulation. Blocking B7 leaves recognition intact but removes signal 2, so the T cells make little IL-2, do not expand, and may be switched into anergy. Drugs of this kind are used to damp T cell attacks on the body's own joints.

variables.name: Binding of naïve T cell receptors to viral peptides in MHC (signal 1)
variables.why: The drug blocks B7, not the MHC–peptide complex, so T cell receptors still find and bind their peptides.

variables.name: Costimulation of those T cells
variables.why: Costimulation is B7 on the dendritic cell binding CD28 on the T cell, and the drug blocks that contact.

variables.name: IL-2 made by the T cells
variables.why: Without signal 2, the T cells are not fully activated and make little IL-2.

variables.name: Number of effector T cells against the virus
variables.why: Little IL-2 means little clonal expansion, so few effector cells form; many of the recognizing cells become anergic instead.

why.correct: The dendritic cell captures antigen at the site of infection, carries it to the lymph node and presents it. A matching naïve T cell receives signal 1 (recognition) and signal 2 (costimulation), makes IL-2, expands, and its effector daughters leave for the tissue.

A dendritic cell that has not sensed a microbe displays peptides but makes little B7. The T cell gets signal 1 without signal 2 and is switched into anergy, a lasting unresponsive state. This is one way self-reactive T cells are held in check outside the thymus.
options: Correct. Signal 1 alone causes anergy.
Expansion needs costimulation as well as recognition, and a resting dendritic cell provides little B7.
Dendritic cells present antigen; they do not release perforin. Perforin is a weapon of cytotoxic T cells and natural killer cells.
Memory T cells form only after full activation and clonal expansion, which have not happened here.

why.correct: Cytotoxic T cells kill by contact. Perforin opens pores, granzymes enter and activate caspases, and Fas ligand triggers the same caspases through Fas. Each route ends in apoptosis.
options: Correct. Perforin forms the pores through which granzymes enter.
T cells do not make antibodies; those come from cells descended from B cells.
Correct. Granzymes activate caspases, which carry out apoptosis.
Engulfing is what phagocytes such as macrophages do. The cytotoxic T cell makes its target die by apoptosis, and a macrophage then engulfs the fragments.
Correct. Fas ligand binding Fas is the granule-free route to apoptosis.
Histamine is released by mast cells and basophils in inflammation, not by T cells.

why.correct: FOXP3 sets up the suppressor program of regulatory T cells. Without them, self-reactive T cells that slipped through negative selection are not suppressed, and they attack the gut, skin and pancreatic beta cells. This rare disease is called IPEX.
options: Losing cytotoxic T cells would cause severe viral infections, not attacks on several of his own organs at once. FOXP3 is the regulatory T cell gene.
Without helper T cells, immune responses would be weak, and he would be prone to infection rather than to attacks on his own tissues.
Correct. Missing regulatory T cells let T cells attack self tissues.
Without dendritic cells, T cells could not be activated at all, which would not cause attacks on his own organs.

why.correct: Without MHC class I, the infected cells cannot show viral peptides to cytotoxic T cells. Natural killer cells attack cells that are missing MHC class I, so they take over.
options: Cytotoxic T cells need viral peptide in MHC class I to recognize a target, and these cells no longer display it.
Helper T cells recognize MHC class II on antigen-presenting cells and do not kill infected cells.
Correct. Missing MHC class I makes a cell a target for natural killer cells.
Regulatory T cells suppress other lymphocytes; they do not kill infected cells.

why.correct: Granzymes and caspases make the target die by apoptosis. It breaks up into tidy fragments that macrophages engulf, so its contents, including virus being assembled inside, are not spilled and there is little inflammation.
options: This step is right. Recognition needs the peptide in MHC class I, bound by the T cell receptor and CD8.
This step is right. Aiming the granules keeps the damage to the one cell being attacked.
This step is right. Perforin opens the way for granzymes.
This step is right. Granzymes trigger the target's own caspases.
This is the error. The target dies by apoptosis, not by bursting.

why.correct: Recognition (signal 1) must be followed by costimulation (signal 2): CD28 on the T cell binding B7 on the presenting cell. Only then does the T cell make IL-2 and expand.
options: Perforin is a weapon released by effector cytotoxic T cells after activation, not a step in activating a naïve cell.
Correct. Costimulation is the second signal.
T cells do not engulf antigen; antigen-presenting cells do that before presentation.
Negative selection happens in the thymus before the T cell ever leaves, not during activation in a lymph node.

why.correct: Th2 cells direct the response to parasitic worms. IL-5 calls up eosinophils, IL-13 increases mucus and speeds turnover of the gut lining, and IL-4 steers B cells and promotes further Th2 development.
options: Th1 cells arm macrophages and cytotoxic T cells against microbes that live inside cells. Interferon gamma actually holds Th2 development back.
Regulatory T cells damp responses down; they do not raise eosinophil numbers.
Cytotoxic T cells are not helper T cells, and a worm is far too large to be killed by granzymes.
Correct. Worms trigger a Th2 response, and IL-5 raises eosinophils.

why.correct: This is graft-versus-host disease. Mature T cells in the donor graft recognize the patient's HLA as foreign and attack the skin, gut and liver. The patient's own immune system was wiped out before the transplant, so nothing stops them.
options: Before a marrow transplant, the patient's immune system is destroyed, so it is poorly placed to reject anything. Rejection would also not target the skin, gut and liver.
Correct. Donor T cells attacking the recipient is graft-versus-host disease.
An ABO mismatch would destroy red cells and cause anemia and dark urine, not this pattern in skin, gut and liver.
Regulatory T cells suppress immune attacks; they do not cause tissue damage.

why.correct: Mature red cells have no nucleus and carry almost no HLA (MHC) proteins, so there is almost nothing for the recipient's T cells to react to. Red cells are matched for their own antigens: ABO, Rh and other blood groups.
options: Antibodies circulate in the plasma alongside red cells and can reach them easily; that is how ABO reactions happen.
Transfused red cells normally survive for weeks. They escape T cells because they lack HLA, not because they are removed early.
HLA types differ greatly between people. The point is that red cells carry almost none.
Correct. Almost no HLA means no tissue typing is needed for red cells.

why.correct: Rejection within minutes is hyperacute rejection. Only antibodies already present, for example against the donor's ABO antigens or HLA, can act that fast. They bind the graft's blood vessel lining, triggering clotting. ABO matching and crossmatching are done to prevent it.
options: Correct. Preformed antibodies cause hyperacute rejection.
T cell rejection needs activation and clonal expansion first, which takes days, not minutes.
Donor T cells attacking the recipient is graft-versus-host disease, which follows marrow transplants and takes weeks.
Scarring of graft arteries is chronic rejection, over months to years.

why.correct: The thymus is where T cells mature. Without it, helper and cytotoxic T cells are missing. B cells are made normally in the marrow, but antibody responses to most protein antigens are weak because helper T cells are absent. Such babies suffer severe viral and fungal infections.

variables.name: Number of mature helper T cells
variables.why: T cells mature in the thymus. Without it, almost no helper T cells are made.

variables.name: Number of mature cytotoxic T cells
variables.why: Cytotoxic T cells also mature in the thymus, so they are missing too.

variables.name: Number of B cells in the blood
variables.why: B cells mature in the red bone marrow, not the thymus, so their numbers are normal.

variables.name: Antibody response to most protein antigens
variables.why: B cells need help from helper T cells to respond well to most protein antigens, and those cells are missing.

variables.name: Ability to kill virus-infected cells by adaptive immunity
variables.why: Without cytotoxic T cells, infected cells showing viral peptides in MHC class I are not killed specifically.

why.correct: Regulatory T cells are CD4 T cells set up by FOXP3. They suppress other lymphocytes with IL-10 and TGF-beta, by taking up IL-2 and by removing B7 from dendritic cells.
options: That describes cytotoxic T cells.
Correct. CD4 marker, suppressor job.
Regulatory T cells are T cells, made in the thymus.
Presenting antigen on MHC class II is the job of antigen-presenting cells such as dendritic cells.

why.correct: Identical twins have identical genes, including their HLA genes. The donor kidney's HLA proteins are the same as the recipient's own, so his T cells treat them as self.
options: Correct. Same HLA, so nothing looks foreign.
Kidney cells carry MHC class I like other nucleated cells, and that is what T cells react to in unrelated grafts.
T cells readily reject kidneys from unrelated donors. Tolerance covers only self HLA.
Twins do share their ABO type, but matching ABO alone prevents only hyperacute rejection. Without matching HLA, T cells would still reject the organ.

why.correct: Apoptosis packs the dying cell into membrane-wrapped fragments. Viral particles still being built inside are destroyed with them, macrophages clear the fragments, and there is little inflammation. A burst cell would spill virus and contents into the tissue.
options: Correct. The virus is contained and cleared with the fragments.
Speed is not the reason: the benefit is what happens to the cell's contents.
Apoptosis is programmed death; the cell does not recover.
The T cell is not harmed either way. It detaches and moves on to kill other targets.

why.correct: The first exposure left memory B cells that outnumber the original naïve cells, respond with less stimulation, and already make switched, better-fitting antibody. When the same antigen returns, they produce plasma cells within days.
options: The graph gives no reason to think the dose changed, and the same pattern appears with identical vaccine doses. Memory, not dose, explains it.
Correct. Memory B cells make the secondary response faster and larger.
Leftover antibody would, if anything, clear some antigen and blunt the response. The rise comes from new plasma cells.
A different antigen would bring a new primary response, with the same lag and low peak as the first. Memory is specific.

why.correct: On a first exposure, only a few naïve B cells fit the antigen. They must be activated, receive helper T cell help, and divide into a clone before plasma cells release enough antibody to measure. That takes about 5–10 days.
options: There are no memory B cells before the first exposure; they are one of its products.
Antigen does reach the B cells. The delay comes from how few matching cells there are and how long expansion takes.
Correct. Clonal selection and expansion cause the lag.
Newly made IgM circulates freely in the plasma and is measurable as soon as enough is made. The lag is real, not hidden antibody.

why.correct: The variable regions of one heavy and one light chain fold together at each arm tip to form the antigen-binding site. They differ from one B cell's antibody to the next, which is what makes each antibody specific.
options: Correct. The variable regions form the binding sites.
The Fc region is made of constant heavy chain regions. It decides what happens after binding, not what is bound.
The hinge gives the arms flexibility, so they can reach antigens at different distances apart. It does not set specificity.
Disulfide bonds hold the chains together. They are the same in every antibody of a class.

why.correct: When IgG binds a microbe with its arm tips, its Fc region points outward. Phagocytes carry Fc receptor proteins that bind that stem, so coated microbes are engulfed far more readily. This is opsonization.
options: Light chains form part of the arms, which are busy gripping the bacterium. They do not bind Fc receptor proteins.
The antigen-binding sites are attached to the bacterium, so they are not free to bind the macrophage.
The variable regions sit at the arm tips, on the bacterium. Receptor proteins on phagocytes bind the constant stem.
Correct. Fc receptor proteins bind the Fc region.

why.correct: A second exposure to the same antigen recalls memory B cells. The response starts sooner, goes higher, is mainly IgG, fits better and leaves more memory cells. That is why boosters work.

variables.name: Days until antibody rises in the blood
variables.why: Memory B cells need less stimulation and are more numerous than the naïve cells were, so plasma cells appear within 1–3 days instead of 5–10.

variables.name: Peak antibody level
variables.why: Many memory B cells each form a clone of plasma cells, so far more antibody is made, often 10 to 100 times more.

variables.name: Share of the antibody that is IgG
variables.why: Memory B cells have already switched class, so the response is mostly IgG, with little of the IgM that starts a primary response.

variables.name: How tightly the antibody binds the toxin
variables.why: Memory cells come from B cells selected for better-fitting antibody during the first responses (affinity maturation).

variables.name: Number of memory B cells afterward
variables.why: Each secondary response makes new memory cells as well as plasma cells, so the pool grows.

why.correct: For a T cell-dependent antigen, the B cell binds antigen, presents its peptides, receives helper T cell help, expands and switches class, and then differentiates into plasma cells, which release antibody, and memory B cells.

Passive immunity is protection by antibody someone else made. Antivenom, maternal IgG, IgA in breast milk and injected anti-D are all borrowed antibody. A vaccine and recovery from infection make your own immune system respond: active immunity.
options: Correct. Antivenom is antibody made in another animal: artificial passive immunity.
A vaccine makes your own B and T cells respond and leave memory: artificial active immunity.
Correct. Maternal IgG is natural passive immunity.
Recovering from an infection is natural active immunity; your own cells made the antibodies and memory cells.
Correct. IgA in milk is natural passive immunity for the baby's gut.
Correct. Injected anti-D is borrowed antibody: artificial passive immunity.

why.correct: IgG carried across from her mother in late pregnancy protected her passively. Borrowed antibody lasts only weeks to months and leaves no memory cells, so as it falls she depends on her own, still inexperienced, immune system.
options: The thymus is large and active throughout infancy and childhood. It does not stop at six months.
Correct. Passive maternal IgG fades over the first months of life.
IgE arms mast cells against worms. Making it would not explain more colds.
Class switching goes from IgM to IgG, IgA or IgE, not to IgD, and it would not remove protection.

why.correct: IgM is the first antibody of a primary response. Finding IgM without IgG means the response has only just begun, so the infection is current or very recent.
options: Correct. IgM comes first, so IgM alone means early in a first response.
An old infection would have left IgG, made after class switching, and little or no IgM.
Vaccine protection years later shows as IgG from memory, not IgM alone.
Only IgG crosses from mother to fetus, and it fades within months of birth. An adult's antibody is his own.

why.correct: Capsule sugars are T cell-independent antigens: they give weak, mostly IgM responses with little memory, and poor ones in young children. A B cell that binds the sugar takes in the whole conjugate and displays peptides from the attached protein on MHC class II. Helper T cells that recognize those peptides then help it expand, switch class and form memory. This is a conjugate vaccine.
options: Size alone does not help. The gain comes from helper T cells, which can then drive class switching and memory.
Protein antigens do need B cells to make antibody. What they add is peptides for helper T cells.
The sugar's lifetime is not the problem. Without T cell help, B cells make a weak response however long the antigen lasts.
Correct. Linking the sugar to a protein turns the response into a T cell-dependent one.

why.correct: Class switching joins the same variable region gene to a different heavy chain constant region gene. The binding site, and so the antigen bound, is unchanged; the stem and its jobs change.
options: The heavy chain constant region is exactly what changes. It defines the class.
Released IgM is a pentamer with ten binding sites; IgG is a monomer with two.
Correct. The variable region is kept, so specificity stays the same.
IgM, not IgG, is the strongest complement activator, so this property changes.

why.correct: This is opsonization. Bound IgG leaves its Fc regions facing out, and phagocytes grab them with Fc receptor proteins, which strongly speeds engulfment.
options: Antibodies do not make holes. The membrane attack complex of complement does.
Correct. Fc receptor proteins link the phagocyte to the coated bacterium.
Bacteria do not have MHC proteins; MHC is found on your own cells.
Antibodies act from outside, on surface antigens. They do not enter bacteria.

why.correct: B cells present engulfed antigen on MHC class II, which is recognized by helper T cells carrying CD4. MHC class I and cytotoxic T cells are for peptides made inside a cell, and a cytotoxic T cell would kill the B cell rather than help it.
options: This step is right. Unlike T cells, B cells bind whole, folded antigens.
This step is right. The B cell processes the antigen it has taken in.
This is the error. B cells present to helper T cells on MHC class II.
This step is right. Helper T cell contact and cytokines activate the B cell.
This step is right. The clone gives both antibody-releasing and memory cells.

why.correct: IgA is the antibody of secretions, including breast milk. Swallowed IgA stays on the gut lining and neutralizes the virus before it can enter cells.
options: IgE sits on mast cells and acts against worms. It is not the protective antibody in milk.
Correct. Secretory IgA guards mucous membranes, including a baby's gut.
IgM is mainly a blood antibody, made early in a first response.
IgD sits on the surface of naïve B cells and is barely released.

why.correct: Released IgM is five Ys joined at their stems, giving ten binding sites. One molecule can bridge several bacteria, so it agglutinates them easily even though each site fits only loosely.
options: Early IgM sites usually fit less tightly than later IgG, because affinity maturation has not happened yet. Its strength is the number of sites.
IgG moves into tissue fluid more easily than bulky IgM.
Every antibody unit has two heavy and two light chains.
Correct. Ten binding sites make IgM the best agglutinator.

why.correct: Antivenom is passive immunity: antibodies made in another animal. They work at once but are broken down within days to weeks, and because his own B cells did not make them, no memory cells formed.
options: Memory B cells come only from your own immune response. Borrowed antibodies do not create them.
Borrowed antibodies last days to a few months, not decades.
Correct. Passive immunity is immediate but temporary.
The answer contradicts itself: if he were immune, he would be protected. Antivenom does not make you immune.

why.correct: Antibodies and complement cannot reach a bacterium inside a macrophage. Th1 helper T cells recognize its peptides on the macrophage's MHC class II and release interferon gamma, which switches the macrophage into a more powerful killer.
options: IgA stops microbes at body surfaces, before they enter. It cannot reach a bacterium inside a cell.
Correct. Th1 cells arm macrophages against bacteria living inside them.
Complement acts on microbes in fluids. Inside a macrophage, the bacterium is out of its reach.
Eosinophils are aimed at worms, which are far too big to live inside a macrophage.

why.correct: Influenza evades immunity by small, steady changes in its surface proteins. Memory cells and antibodies from earlier years fit the new version less well, so the vaccine is updated each season. Measles surface proteins barely change, so memory keeps working.
options: Correct. Changing antigens is a form of immune evasion.
Influenza vaccines do produce memory cells. The problem is that the virus changes.
It is chickenpox virus that hides in nerve cells. And if measles hid, a vaccine would work worse, not better.
People make plenty of IgG against influenza; that IgG targets last year's version.

why.correct: IgG is the only class actively carried across to the fetus, mostly in late pregnancy. It protects the newborn for months, and it is why maternal anti-D can harm an Rh-positive fetus.
options: IgM is a large pentamer and does not cross.
IgA reaches the baby after birth, in breast milk, but does not cross in pregnancy.
IgE does not cross.
Correct. IgG is the only class that crosses.

why.correct: Antibody actions split by the part of the antibody they use. Neutralization and agglutination depend on the variable regions and still work. Opsonization depends on phagocytes binding the Fc region, so it fails.

variables.name: Binding of IgG to the bacterium
variables.why: IgG binds with its variable regions, which the drug does not touch.

variables.name: Phagocytes engulfing IgG-coated bacteria
variables.why: Phagocytes grab coated bacteria by binding the IgG Fc regions, and those receptor proteins are blocked.

variables.name: Neutralization of the toxin by antibody
variables.why: Neutralization only needs antibody covering the toxin's binding site, which uses the variable regions.

variables.name: Agglutination of the bacteria
variables.why: Clumping depends on antibodies bridging bacteria with their binding sites, not on phagocytes.

why.correct: Plasma cells are fully differentiated B cells built for export: their rough endoplasmic reticulum makes antibody, about 2,000 molecules per second.
options: Memory B cells are resting cells that wait for a later exposure. They release little antibody until they become plasma cells.
Helper T cells release cytokines, not antibody.
Correct. Plasma cells are the antibody factories.
A naïve B cell carries antibody on its surface as its B cell receptor but does not release it in bulk.

why.correct: Body-wide mast cell degranulation lowers TPR and plasma volume, so venous return and MAP fall into distributive shock. The baroreceptor reflex speeds the heart, and airway smooth muscle contracts. The immune trigger reaches the circulation, the nervous system's reflexes and breathing.

variables.name: Histamine and leukotrienes in the blood
variables.why: Venom cross-links IgE on mast cells and basophils throughout the body, and they degranulate at once.

variables.name: Total peripheral resistance (TPR)
variables.why: Histamine and leukotrienes relax the smooth muscle of arterioles, which widen.

variables.name: Plasma volume
variables.why: The mediators make capillaries and venules leak, and plasma moves into the tissues.

variables.name: Venous return
variables.why: Plasma is lost from the vessels and blood pools in widened veins, so less returns to the heart.

variables.name: Mean arterial pressure
variables.why: MAP = CO × TPR, and TPR falls while cardiac output falls with venous return.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: Lower MAP reduces baroreceptor firing, so the cardiovascular center raises sympathetic output to the SA node.

variables.name: Airway diameter
variables.why: Mediators contract airway smooth muscle and swell the airway lining.

why.correct: Epinephrine reverses each part of anaphylaxis through a different adrenergic receptor protein: alpha-1 constricts vessels and cuts leak, beta-1 strengthens the heart, and beta-2 relaxes the airways and damps mast cells. MAP and breathing recover.

variables.name: TPR
variables.why: Epinephrine on alpha-1 receptor proteins contracts arteriolar smooth muscle.

variables.name: Leak of plasma from capillaries
variables.why: Alpha-1 constriction lowers the pressure and flow into leaky vessels, and less mediator is released, so less plasma escapes.

variables.name: Contractility of the ventricles
variables.why: Epinephrine on beta-1 receptor proteins raises calcium entry in heart muscle cells.

variables.name: Airway diameter
variables.why: Epinephrine on beta-2 receptor proteins relaxes airway smooth muscle.

variables.name: Further mediator release from mast cells
variables.why: Beta-2 stimulation raises cyclic AMP in mast cells, which damps degranulation.

variables.name: Mean arterial pressure
variables.why: TPR, venous return and cardiac output all rise, so MAP rises.

why.correct: Helper T cells coordinate almost every adaptive response. As HIV destroys them, cytotoxic and antibody responses fail, the virus climbs again, and opportunistic infections define AIDS.

variables.name: CD4 count in the blood
variables.why: HIV enters cells through CD4, and infected and bystander helper T cells die faster than they are replaced.

variables.name: Cytotoxic T cell response to a new virus
variables.why: Cytotoxic T cells need helper T cell IL-2 and licensed dendritic cells to expand strongly.

variables.name: Class-switched antibody made against a new protein antigen
variables.why: B cells need helper T cell contact and cytokines to respond to protein antigens and to switch class.

variables.name: Infections by microbes that rarely trouble healthy people
variables.why: With both arms of adaptive immunity weakened, opportunistic fungi, viruses and bacteria can grow.

variables.name: Amount of HIV in the blood
variables.why: As helper T cells collapse, cytotoxic T cells lose their help and no longer hold the virus down.

why.correct: In the chronic phase, cytotoxic T cells hold the virus at a steady level, but never clear it, and the CD4 count declines year after year. Symptoms are few until the count gets low.
options: The virus line never reaches zero, and the CD4 line slopes down, not up.
Correct. A steady virus level and a slowly falling CD4 count mark the chronic phase.
The pattern is the reverse: the CD4 count falls and the virus stays roughly level.
Only the virus rises, and only late. The CD4 count falls throughout this stretch.

why.correct: Within a few weeks, HIV-specific cytotoxic T cells expand and kill infected cells, and the virus falls to a steady level. Antibodies appear around the same time (seroconversion) but do little to control the virus, which mutates around them.
options: Fewer cells to infect may contribute, but the drop matches the arrival of HIV-specific cytotoxic T cells, and removing those cells in animal studies makes the virus climb again.
The graph shows untreated infection. The drop happens without drugs.
Correct. Cytotoxic T cells lower the virus to its steady level.
The CD4 count only partly recovers, to about 750, and does not return to its starting level.

why.correct: A rash that takes one to three days to appear, at the site of contact, in someone sensitized before, is delayed hypersensitivity. Memory Th1 cells gather at the site, release cytokines and call in macrophages, and cytotoxic T cells kill skin cells displaying the altered proteins.
options: Type I reactions begin within minutes, not days.
Type II needs antibody against a fixed cell-surface antigen; this rash is caused by T cells.
Type III involves soluble immune complexes lodging in vessels, joints and kidneys, not a rash exactly where a plant touched.
Correct. The two-day delay points to T cells.

why.correct: Hay fever is type I hypersensitivity. Sensitization has already armed mast cells in the nasal lining with pollen-specific IgE. Pollen links two IgE molecules, and within seconds the mast cells release histamine and other mediators: sneezing, itching, a running nose.
options: Correct. Cross-linking IgE on sensitized mast cells triggers degranulation.
Killing by cytotoxic T cells is part of type IV, which takes days. Hay fever starts within minutes.
Immune complexes in the kidneys are type III, not an allergy of the nose.
A first meeting would cause sensitization without symptoms. Symptoms come from later exposures.

why.correct: In type II hypersensitivity, IgG or IgM binds an antigen fixed on a cell. Recipient antibodies destroy donor red cells, maternal anti-D destroys fetal red cells, and antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor protein and the TSH receptor protein change how those receptor proteins work.
options: Correct. Recipient anti-A or anti-B bind the donor red cells.
Poison ivy rash is type IV, caused by T cells over days.
Correct. Antibodies against acetylcholine receptor proteins reduce their number.
Hay fever is type I, IgE on mast cells.
Correct. An antibody switches on the TSH receptor protein.
Correct. Maternal anti-D binds the fetus's red cells.

why.correct: An allergy needs a first, symptom-free exposure. The first sting triggered Th2 help and class switching to venom-specific IgE, which coated his mast cells. The second sting cross-linked that IgE and triggered widespread degranulation.
options: The dose of a single sting varies little. The change is in his immune system, not the bee.
IgM does not arm mast cells, and blocking the venom would prevent a reaction, not cause one.
Mast cells release histamine from birth. What was missing was venom-specific IgE on them.
Correct. Sensitization on the first exposure sets up the reaction on the next.

why.correct: Anaphylaxis is driven by several mediators, including leukotrienes, that antihistamines do not block. Antihistamines take time to act and cannot constrict vessels, strengthen the heart or relax airway smooth muscle. Epinephrine does all three.
options: Correct. Its action is narrow and slow; epinephrine is essential.
Antihistamines block histamine's receptor proteins; they do not increase its release.
Antihistamines do not block adrenergic receptor proteins, so they do not interfere with epinephrine.
Antihistamines relieve itching and hives anywhere on the body. Their limit is that they do not treat shock or airway narrowing.

why.correct: This is anaphylaxis with shock. Intramuscular epinephrine into the outer thigh raises TPR and cuts leak (alpha-1), supports the heart (beta-1) and widens the airways (beta-2). Fluids, oxygen and lying flat support it.
options: An antihistamine is slow, blocks only histamine and does not treat shock or airway narrowing.
Corticosteroids take hours to act and do not reverse the immediate problem.
Correct. Epinephrine is the first-line treatment.
Her fast heart rate is the baroreceptor reflex holding up cardiac output. A beta blocker would worsen shock and block epinephrine's effects.

why.correct: Antibodies have reduced her acetylcholine receptor proteins, so each end plate potential is smaller and the normal safety margin is gone. With repeated firing, each impulse releases a little less acetylcholine, and more and more fibers fail to reach threshold.
options: Her motor neurons release acetylcholine normally. The fault is at the receptor proteins on the muscle side.
Her acetylcholinesterase is normal. Drugs that inhibit it actually help her.
Her muscle fibers are normal when they are excited. The failure is in transmission at the end plate.
Correct. Fewer receptor proteins leave no safety margin as acetylcholine release falls with use.

why.correct: Pyridostigmine blocks acetylcholinesterase, so each release of acetylcholine lingers and binds more of the remaining receptor proteins. The end plate potential gets larger and more often reaches threshold.
options: Correct. It slows acetylcholine breakdown.
Removing the thymus can help some patients, but pyridostigmine acts at the end plate, not on the thymus.
It does not touch the antibodies; immunosuppressant drugs lower their production.
It cannot make new receptor proteins. It makes better use of those that remain.

why.correct: Sensitization comes first: Th2 help and IL-4 switch B cells to IgE, which arms mast cells. A later exposure cross-links that IgE, the mast cells degranulate, and histamine and other mediators cause the symptoms.
Histamine and leukotrienes dilate arterioles, so TPR falls. That is why anaphylactic shock is a distributive shock, and why epinephrine's alpha-1 constriction helps.
options: This step is right. Body-wide degranulation starts anaphylaxis.
This is the error. The mediators dilate arterioles, lowering TPR.
This step is right. Leaky vessels lose plasma into the tissues.
This step is right. Less volume and pooled blood reduce venous return and output.
This step is right. Low MAP means too little oxygen delivery: shock.

why.correct: Beta-2 receptor proteins raise cyclic AMP in smooth muscle, which relaxes it. The airways widen and wheezing eases.
options: Contraction would narrow the airways. Beta-2 means smooth muscle relaxes; alpha-1 is the receptor protein that contracts it.
Correct. Beta-2 stimulation relaxes airway smooth muscle.
Beta-2 stimulation damps mast cell release rather than increasing it.
Epinephrine constricts vessels in the airway lining through alpha-1, which reduces swelling.

why.correct: In lupus, antibodies bind nuclear antigens, including DNA, released from dying cells. The immune complexes circulate and lodge in small vessels, joints, serous membranes, skin and the kidneys' filters, where complement and neutrophils inflame them: type III hypersensitivity.
options: IgE on mast cells causes type I allergy, which comes and goes in minutes, not lasting inflammation in many organs.
Correct. Circulating immune complexes can lodge almost anywhere.
A T cell attack on one organ's protein would damage that organ only, as in type 1 diabetes.
Lupus is autoimmune, not an infection. The antibodies target the body's own nuclear contents.

why.correct: IgG carried across from his mother protected him for the first months. It fades over weeks to months and leaves no memory. Because he has no working T cells, he cannot make his own adaptive response, so infections begin as the borrowed IgG runs out.
options: Correct. Fading maternal IgG unmasks the missing T cells.
In healthy babies the thymus makes T cells well before birth. In SCID the T cells never develop at all.

First vaccines are given at 2 months, and a single vaccine would not explain one severe infection after another with many kinds of microbe. (A live vaccine, such as oral rotavirus vaccine, can itself make a baby with SCID ill.) The timing matches the loss of maternal antibody.
His B cells were never able to make useful antibody without helper T cells; that did not change at 4 months.

why.correct: PD-1 is a brake that keeps some T cells, including some self-reactive ones, switched off. Blocking it lets T cells attack the tumor, but self-reactive T cells are freed as well, so healthy organs such as the thyroid and gut can be attacked.
options: The damage is done by T cells, not by the drug acting on those cells directly.
This is a T cell attack on self tissue, not a type I reaction.
Spread of the tumor would not explain inflammation of these organs right after the drug started.
Correct. Checkpoint inhibitors can break self-tolerance.

why.correct: AIDS is the late stage of HIV infection, diagnosed when the CD4 count falls below 200 per microliter or when an AIDS-defining illness, such as Pneumocystis lung infection or Kaposi sarcoma, appears.
options: A positive antibody test shows HIV infection, which can be years from AIDS.
A normal CD4 count is about 500 to 1,500 per microliter, so values below 1,000 are often normal.
Fever and swollen lymph nodes have many causes, including the acute phase of HIV itself, and do not define AIDS.
Correct. CD4 below 200, or a defining illness.

why.correct: This is rheumatic fever, an example of molecular mimicry. A strep surface protein resembles proteins in heart valves and joints, so antibodies and T cells made against the bacterium cross-react with the child's own tissue.
options: In rheumatic fever the valve is inflamed without bacteria in it. The delay of weeks points to an immune response, not spread of the infection.
An allergic reaction would begin in minutes. A delay of weeks fits the time needed to make antibodies.
Correct. Cross-reacting antibodies attack self tissue that resembles the microbe.
Strep does not destroy regulatory T cells. The attack is aimed at a specific look-alike protein.

why.correct: Rheumatoid arthritis is a systemic autoimmune disease. T cells, B cells and cytokines such as TNF inflame the synovial membranes, which erode cartilage and bone, typically in the small joints of both hands and feet.
options: Wear and tear with age describes a different, non-autoimmune joint disease. Rheumatoid arthritis is immune-driven and can start young.
Correct. Autoimmune, synovial, usually symmetric small joints.
IgE and pollen cause hay fever, not joint disease.
A single joint after injury is not the pattern of rheumatoid arthritis, which is symmetric and has no injury behind it.
